name: Nora Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work for the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, unions, AI companies, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play cello in a city chamber group, record short lines and teach five pupils. I have a music bachelor’s and enough years to lead a rehearsal when asked, though I am an ordinary section player. I like listening for the moment a young player finally hears the whole phrase; I dislike chasing a fee after the concert.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does work support home at this point?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, my partner works at a pharmacy and our grown children live away. We have a small mortgage and four months of expenses saved, built from typical music pay; a few ensembles hire nearby. I use AI every day to draft routes and rehearsal lists, but I check paid calls and pupil information myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the chamber group that a quicker rehearsal list is useful if it still shows the player’s fee. I would check the printed calls before travelling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The concert run, five pupils and my partner’s pharmacy wage are steady this term. Four months saved covers an ordinary gap, although the mortgage still takes a careful calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep paid concerts, recordings and five pupils, and ask for the next run’s rehearsal and cancellation fees in writing. In the first plateau year I would request my actual pension estimate before naming any retirement date and save one fifth of cleared extra recording fees after mortgage, food and travel toward six months of bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our income in this picture. A signed concert fee is easier to plan around than a hopeful enquiry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check on the rehearsal list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The time, fee and travel gap between venues. An AI draft can put two calls across town at the same hour, so I compare it with signed dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop playing at 60?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not have an actual pension figure yet. My partner and I would read the estimate with our bills before choosing a date.

think: Our **four-month reserve** covers an ordinary gap between the current paid concert runs.

do: Keep **concerts, recordings and pupils** with written rehearsal and cancellation fees.
Request **actual pension estimate**; save fifth of cleared extra recordings after essentials toward six months.
feel: I feel **calm** about current work and household bills.

fieldNote: Her **four-month reserve** and two current incomes support calm in a plateau.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the musicians’ association to show which recording and rehearsal hours remain paid. I would tell the group that a live cello phrase still takes a player listening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect short recording calls to thin and perhaps a paid planning hour to go. They are nearly a quarter of my own pay, and four months saved would not restore that line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would take last season’s paid hours to the association and ask for a written rehearsal minimum, while keeping concerts and five pupils. If two monthly recording calls disappear, I would seek a posted paid ensemble-coordination role only if my music bachelor’s and rehearsal experience meet its requirements, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the bus schedule works; I would keep music until a signed offer, including in the first disruption year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a real part of my income shrinking. I can negotiate and apply, but I cannot pay the mortgage with a meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the association bring to the hall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paid calls, the hours spent preparing and the cancelled dates. I want a written rate, not a speech about valuing musicians.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you upload a pupil recording for a faster list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I keep pupil audio private unless a family gives written permission. The existing calendar draft does not need their voices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the group that 2028 thinking AGI could make bookings and cello tracks before robot players arrive around 2031. I would ask for signed paid concert dates now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect short recording orders to end and some rehearsal planning fees to disappear in 2028. That is a noticeable share of my income; live playing may continue, but four months saved is not a replacement wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I would get written paid concert dates and keep five pupils. In the first year after 2028, if recordings end and rehearsal pay also falls, I would apply for a posted paid ensemble-coordinator role only if my music bachelor’s and rehearsal leadership meet its requirements, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and transport fits; I would keep concerts and pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a fast pay cut, though some nearby ensembles and four months saved let me look for a real opening. The reserve is a bridge, not a new salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the association guarantee your contract?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. It can argue for fair terms, but the ensemble has to sign and pay them. I would keep track of the actual deposits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why mention the later robot date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robot cello playing is around 2031 in this card. Booking and recorded lines may change in 2028, which is the first date my invoices could move.

Seek **posted coordinator role** after both 2028 recording/rehearsal losses; accepted music bachelor’s/leadership, written replacement net after travel and workable transport.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the association that five years lets musicians seek fair pay for both rehearsal and recorded use. Thinking AGI arrives around 2031 and robot cellists around 2034 in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Recorded lines may lose buyers by 2031. I could learn live sound for a different paid role, but a free course without hours I can bill would hurt the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep concerts and pupils and check actual posted paid sound-assistant roles. If two monthly recording calls disappear, I would take a live-sound certificate course only after a real funded place on paid time is confirmed, a posted employer recognises the certificate, and the timetable preserves my current paid lessons and bus home; in the first year after 2031 I would move only if written net pay after travel replaces lost fees, transport works and a signed offer arrives, retaining music until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about recording income over the next few years, but five years lets me compare a real course and job. I will not trade a paid cello lesson for an unrecognised live-sound certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you run a concert sound desk alone after the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would do the first checks with a venue technician and wait for signed equipment and safety clearance before handling a crowded show alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who covers your course hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The funded place must include paid hours and leave my paid pupil time intact. If that fails, I keep the music week I have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that thinking AGI around 2036 and robot cellists around 2039 are separate dates. I would still ask the hall what a rehearsal and recording use pays today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may choose fewer concerts, but I have not set a retirement date without a pension estimate. The current concert run and pharmacy wage make the next few years steady enough, while four months saved cannot cover a distant loss forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep concerts and five pupils, request my actual pension estimate and save one fifth of cleared extra recording fees after mortgage, food and travel toward six months. Across the decade I would ask the association for written rehearsal and recorded-use rates; in the first year after 2036, if recordings and rehearsals lose fees, I would seek a posted paid ensemble-coordinator role only if my music bachelor’s and rehearsal leadership qualify, written net pay after travel replaces lost income and transport works, keeping current music until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about distant recording pay while present bookings and my partner’s wage hold the mortgage. A decade helps us ask for better terms, not assume they have been paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you count pension money now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would request the actual estimate and put it next to our bills, not treat an unknown figure as a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the association gets no new rate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid concerts and pupils while they are offered and apply only to real posted jobs if fees fall. A musicians’ association fee meeting is not a paid contract.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because recording and planning fees could fall before I find a new paid role. Signed concert dates, an actual posted job accepting my degree and a written net wage after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who keeps earning when a recorded cello line is used again. A single session fee can disappear into a thousand plays if nobody writes the rights down.

headlineQuote: A single session fee can disappear into a thousand plays if nobody writes the rights down.
portrait: Nora is an **experienced cellist** with a music bachelor’s, five pupils and ordinary local pay.
She has **four months saved**, a pharmacy-working partner, grown children and a mortgage.
She uses **AI daily** for lists but checks paid calls and pupil information herself.
She seeks **collective pay terms** and a funded, paid live-sound route only after real recording losses.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could cut recording and planning fees before a new paid role is available.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **signed concert dates**, a posted role accepting her degree and written replacement net after travel.
